content: 1. A comprehensive framework should be established to map policies, including legislation, regulations, guidelines, and standards, that influence wheelchair provision. This will help identify gaps, barriers, and opportunities in policy. 2. The results of this mapping should be used to prioritize the development or strengthening of policies to ensure effective, seamless, and sustainable wheelchair provision. 3. A unified framework for collecting wheelchair provision data should be developed. This framework should include indicators of quality and sustainability to evaluate progress and improve service provision. 4. Feedback loops are essential for improving the quality and suitability of available wheelchair products. These loops should allow for reporting product failures or performance issues and can be integrated into follow-up wheelchair services or facilitated through digital technology. 5. Clear and accessible information about wheelchair products and their features should be made available to service providers and users. This will aid in informed decision-making and product selection. Suppliers should be required to provide detailed product information, and training for service personnel on product features should be incorporated into service delivery training. 6. Member States should identify a minimum range of wheelchairs to be made available as part of Universal Health Coverage (UHC). This can be based on the WHO Priority Assistive Product List and integrated into national priority assistive product lists. 7. Member States are encouraged to develop quality and safety standards for wheelchairs. These standards will guide procurement and signal industry requirements. Collaboration with government regulators, manufacturers, and clinicians is recommended, using existing international standards and adapting them to national contexts. 8. Processes for certifying products against these standards should be accessible, achievable, and affordable. 9. Sharing best practice examples of cost-effective wheelchair provision solutions can inform national planning. These examples, supported by evidence and research, should be made available through a central portal, with WHO and other stakeholders facilitating dissemination. 10. Developing protocols and clinical practice guidelines tailored to the main groups of wheelchair users can enhance decision-making and efficiency within health and service systems. These tools should provide clear guidance on identifying needs, referral processes, risk factors, and special requirements for specific groups. 11. At an early stage of developing national wheelchair provision systems, Member States should receive guidance on the roles of personnel at different levels of health and service systems and the resources required for these roles. 12. A competency framework for wheelchair provision roles should be developed. This framework will inform workforce planning, support training curriculum development, and facilitate recognition and accreditation of training programs and individuals. 13. Active collaboration with wheelchair service user groups is essential to increase awareness and demand for appropriate wheelchairs. This includes engaging user representatives in decision-making and providing information and training on relevant issues. 14. Despite significant growth in wheelchair provision research since 2008, extensive gaps remain. Further research is needed to provide better data and evidence on effective practices, enabling more specific and authoritative guidance for policymakers and stakeholders. 15. Research should address gaps in service delivery, including the clinical implementation of service steps, training for users and assistants, follow-up frequency and methods, and reporting outcomes of service steps. 16. The impact of policy and funding on the availability and provision of appropriate wheelchairs, as well as on the accessibility and utilization of service delivery steps, should be studied. 17. Methods to reduce inequity in the availability, access, and utilization of wheelchair services, as well as in the harms and benefits experienced by users, should be explored. 18. Population-level estimates of met and unmet needs for wheelchairs, as well as the availability, access, and utilization of services, should be determined. 19. Health system interventions that improve the ability of healthcare providers to identify wheelchair needs and increase referrals to services should be developed. 20. Definitions of timely wheelchair service delivery from the perspective of users should be established, providing benchmarks for performance. 21. Comprehensive financial and economic evaluations of service-level recommendations, including program costs, cost-effectiveness, and cost-benefit analyses, should be conducted. 22. Examples and methods of monitoring, evaluation, and performance improvement that reduce harms and improve benefits for wheelchair users and service providers should be documented. 23. The development of a competency and outcomes framework that bridges education and employment for all wheelchair service roles is necessary. This framework should guide education programs, provide performance benchmarks, and inform in-service skills development and capacity building.
